zh.fullModernText:
把一根粗木棍折断并不容易，这说明原子或分子间的相互作用可以很强。
木棍也是由分子组成的。
实际尝试应由成人安全操作，注意木刺和断裂碎片，不要徒手冒险。

在这里讨论的简化分子模型中，如果没有分子间的吸引，分子就不能聚在一起形成液体或固体，只能像气体那样分散。
吸引力使分子彼此靠近，是形成液体和固体的重要条件。
但只有吸引力，还不能使原子和分子的排列保持稳定。

分子靠得很近时，排斥作用会显著增强。
它阻碍分子继续挤近，阻止它们无限地挤入彼此内部。

原子有电子和原子核，分子由原子组成，内部结构更复杂。
电子和原子核带有电荷，邻近分子中的这些粒子会相互作用。
即使分子整体呈电中性，近距离的电相互作用也可能很强。

完整描述这些粒子的运动和分子间的力，是原子物理学研究的复杂问题。
这需要量子理论，不能只用固定不动的电荷来解释。
这里不讨论内部运动的细节，只根据这些研究的结果，用简化模型说明两个分子间的合力怎样随中心距离变化。

原子和分子内部有带异号电荷的粒子。
在这里的简化模型中，原子间或分子间的相互作用用吸引和排斥两部分表示。

这两部分方向相反。
沿两中心连线取排斥方向为正时，合力的投影等于排斥力的大小减去吸引力的大小，正负号表示方向。

在这个模型描述的近距离范围内，原子越靠近，排斥作用增长得比吸引作用更快①。
当原子或分子的电子层开始重叠时，排斥作用尤其急剧地增强。

① 准确地说，这里比较的是力在两个原子中心连线上的投影。
这个投影带正负号，用来表示力沿连线的方向。

图 $5$ 示意了排斥力（上方曲线）、吸引力（下方曲线）和合力（中间曲线）随两个分子中心距离变化的大致关系。
沿中心连线取排斥方向为正，所以排斥力的投影为正，吸引力的投影为负。
在这个模型中，平衡距离约等于两个分子半径之和 $r_0$，此时两种力的大小相等，合力 $F=0$。

当 $r>r_0$ 时，吸引力较强，所以 $F<0$，合力使分子靠近。
如果 $r\to\infty$，那么 $F\to0$，也就是相距无限远时相互作用趋于零。
当 $r<r_0$ 时，排斥力较强，所以 $F>0$，合力使分子分开。

图 5

分子间合力随距离的变化，可以说明物体受压或受拉时为什么会产生弹性力。
如果分子间的距离被压到小于 $r_0$，排斥占优势，合力阻碍它们进一步靠近。
如果把原本靠近平衡位置的分子稍微拉开，吸引就占优势，合力会促使它们靠近。

在小而可恢复的弹性形变范围内，外界作用停止后，这种恢复作用使分子趋向初始位置。
这不表示任意远离的分子都会自行返回，物体若已断裂也不适用这个结论。

当分子间的距离超过分子本身大小的几倍时，在这里讨论的中性分子模型中，相互作用通常已很弱，实际上可以忽略。
这种力因此称为短程作用力，并不是说它在某个距离处突然变成零。

分子只偏离平衡位置很小时，无论吸引还是排斥占优势，合力都指向平衡位置，其大小近似随偏离距离线性增大。
图 $5$ 中合力曲线的粗线段很短，可以近似看作直线段。

因此，在小形变的弹性范围内，胡克定律近似成立，即弹性力的大小与形变成正比。
分子偏离平衡位置较大时，曲线的弯曲不能忽略，胡克定律的线性近似就不再适用。

物体发生形变时，许多相邻分子层之间的距离都会改变，总形变分散在这些分子层之间。
只要分到每一层的距离变化仍很小，局部的线性近似就仍然适用。

因此，即使物体的总形变超过分子大小的百万倍，胡克定律仍可能成立，条件是形变仍在弹性范围内。
总形变的长度很大，不代表每一层的距离变化也很大。

en.fullModernText:
A thick wooden stick is hard to break, showing that the forces between its atoms or molecules can be strong.
The stick, too, is made of molecules.
Any attempt to break it should be handled safely by an adult, with care to avoid splinters and flying fragments.

In the simplified molecular model discussed here, molecules without mutual attraction could not gather into liquids or solids and would remain dispersed like a gas.
Attraction keeps molecules close together and is an important condition for forming liquids and solids.

Attraction alone, however, cannot keep the arrangement of atoms and molecules stable.
Repulsion becomes strong when molecules are very close.
It resists further compression and prevents them from being pushed indefinitely into one another.

Atoms contain electrons and nuclei, while molecules have still more complex structures built from atoms.
Electrons and nuclei carry electric charge, so those in neighboring molecules interact.

Even a molecule with no overall charge can have strong electrical interactions at short distances.
Describing the motion of these particles and the forces between molecules is a complex problem studied in atomic physics.

A full account requires quantum theory, not just a picture of fixed electric charges.
Here we use the results of that theory only to outline how the force between two molecules depends on their center-to-center distance.

Atoms and molecules contain particles with opposite electric charges.
In this simplified model, their interactions are represented by an attractive part and a repulsive part.

These parts act in opposite directions.
With the direction of repulsion taken as positive, the net force component is the repulsive magnitude minus the attractive magnitude, and its sign gives the direction.

Within the short-distance range described by this model, repulsion increases faster than attraction as atoms move closer together①.
Repulsion rises especially steeply when the electron shells of atoms or molecules begin to overlap.

① More precisely, we are comparing the components of the forces along the line joining the centers of the two atoms.
These signed components indicate direction along that line.

Figure $5$ sketches the approximate dependence of repulsion (upper curve), attraction (lower curve), and the net force (middle curve) on the distance between molecular centers.
Taking repulsion as the positive direction along the line of centers makes the repulsive component positive and the attractive component negative.

In this model, the equilibrium distance is approximately the sum of the two molecular radii, $r_0$, where the two force magnitudes are equal and the net force is $F=0$.
When $r>r_0$, attraction is stronger, so $F<0$ and the net force pulls the molecules closer together.

If $r\to\infty$, then $F\to0$: the interaction tends to zero as the separation tends to infinity.
When $r<r_0$, repulsion is stronger, so $F>0$ and the net force pushes the molecules apart.

Figure 5

The way the net intermolecular force varies with distance helps explain elastic forces in a compressed or stretched body.
If compression reduces the molecular separation below $r_0$, repulsion is stronger and the net force resists further approach.

If molecules initially near equilibrium are pulled slightly apart, attraction is stronger and the net force draws them closer.
For a small, recoverable elastic deformation, this restoring action tends to bring the molecules back toward their initial positions after the external action stops.
This does not mean that arbitrarily distant molecules will return on their own, or that the same conclusion applies to a broken body.

In this model of neutral molecules, the interaction usually becomes negligible when their separation is more than several times their size.
Intermolecular forces of this kind are short-range forces, meaning that they rapidly become weak rather than stopping abruptly at a fixed distance.

When molecules move only a little from equilibrium, the net force points back toward equilibrium.
Its magnitude grows approximately in proportion to the displacement, whether attraction or repulsion is stronger.

The short, thick segment of the net-force curve in Figure $5$ can therefore be treated as approximately straight.
Thus Hooke's law is a useful approximation for small elastic deformations: the magnitude of the elastic force is proportional to the deformation.
For larger molecular displacements, the curve's bending matters and this linear approximation no longer applies.

When a body deforms, the separations of many neighboring molecular layers change, distributing the total deformation across those layers.
The change between any pair of neighboring layers can therefore remain very small.

This is why Hooke's law can still apply even when the total deformation exceeds a million times the size of a molecule, provided each layer's change stays small and the deformation remains elastic.
A large total change in length does not mean a large change in each intermolecular separation.

blocks.source_text: 分子相互作用力与它们之间的距离的关系，可以解释当物体压缩和拉伸时出现的弹性力。如果迫使分子间的距离小于 $r_0$，就产生阻碍接近的力。相反，当分子被扯远离时，就产生了吸引力，当外界作用停止之后，这个吸引力使分子回到初始位置。

blocks.text:
In this model of neutral molecules, the interaction usually becomes negligible when their separation is more than several times their size.
Intermolecular forces of this kind are short-range forces, meaning that they rapidly become weak rather than stopping abruptly at a fixed distance.
blocks.source_text: 如果分子间的距离超过它们的大小几倍，那么分子间的相互作用实际上就不明显了。分子力是短程作用力。

blocks.text:
When molecules move only a little from equilibrium, the net force points back toward equilibrium.
Its magnitude grows approximately in proportion to the displacement, whether attraction or repulsion is stronger.

The short, thick segment of the net-force curve in Figure $5$ can therefore be treated as approximately straight.
Thus Hooke's law is a useful approximation for small elastic deformations: the magnitude of the elastic force is proportional to the deformation.
For larger molecular displacements, the curve's bending matters and this linear approximation no longer applies.
blocks.source_text: 当分子移开平衡位置很小时，吸引力或排斥力随着位移的增大而线性地增大。曲线上很小的一段可以认为是直线段（图 $5$ 上曲线的粗线段）。因此，当形变小的时候，胡克定律是正确的，即弹性力与形变成正比。当分子移动大时，胡克定律就不正确了。

blocks.text:
When a body deforms, the separations of many neighboring molecular layers change, distributing the total deformation across those layers.
The change between any pair of neighboring layers can therefore remain very small.

This is why Hooke's law can still apply even when the total deformation exceeds a million times the size of a molecule, provided each layer's change stays small and the deformation remains elastic.
A large total change in length does not mean a large change in each intermolecular separation.
blocks.source_text: 因为当物体形变时，所有分子之间的距离都改变，所以，总的形变分到相邻分子层上的是很小的。因此，当形变超过分子大小的百万倍时，胡克定律仍然成立。

fullText.zh:
把一根粗木棍折断并不容易，这说明原子或分子间的相互作用可以很强。
木棍也是由分子组成的。
实际尝试应由成人安全操作，注意木刺和断裂碎片，不要徒手冒险。

在这里讨论的简化分子模型中，如果没有分子间的吸引，分子就不能聚在一起形成液体或固体，只能像气体那样分散。
吸引力使分子彼此靠近，是形成液体和固体的重要条件。
但只有吸引力，还不能使原子和分子的排列保持稳定。

分子靠得很近时，排斥作用会显著增强。
它阻碍分子继续挤近，阻止它们无限地挤入彼此内部。

原子有电子和原子核，分子由原子组成，内部结构更复杂。
电子和原子核带有电荷，邻近分子中的这些粒子会相互作用。
即使分子整体呈电中性，近距离的电相互作用也可能很强。

完整描述这些粒子的运动和分子间的力，是原子物理学研究的复杂问题。
这需要量子理论，不能只用固定不动的电荷来解释。
这里不讨论内部运动的细节，只根据这些研究的结果，用简化模型说明两个分子间的合力怎样随中心距离变化。

原子和分子内部有带异号电荷的粒子。
在这里的简化模型中，原子间或分子间的相互作用用吸引和排斥两部分表示。

这两部分方向相反。
沿两中心连线取排斥方向为正时，合力的投影等于排斥力的大小减去吸引力的大小，正负号表示方向。

在这个模型描述的近距离范围内，原子越靠近，排斥作用增长得比吸引作用更快①。
当原子或分子的电子层开始重叠时，排斥作用尤其急剧地增强。

① 准确地说，这里比较的是力在两个原子中心连线上的投影。
这个投影带正负号，用来表示力沿连线的方向。

图 $5$ 示意了排斥力（上方曲线）、吸引力（下方曲线）和合力（中间曲线）随两个分子中心距离变化的大致关系。
沿中心连线取排斥方向为正，所以排斥力的投影为正，吸引力的投影为负。
在这个模型中，平衡距离约等于两个分子半径之和 $r_0$，此时两种力的大小相等，合力 $F=0$。

当 $r>r_0$ 时，吸引力较强，所以 $F<0$，合力使分子靠近。
如果 $r\to\infty$，那么 $F\to0$，也就是相距无限远时相互作用趋于零。
当 $r<r_0$ 时，排斥力较强，所以 $F>0$，合力使分子分开。

图 5

分子间合力随距离的变化，可以说明物体受压或受拉时为什么会产生弹性力。
如果分子间的距离被压到小于 $r_0$，排斥占优势，合力阻碍它们进一步靠近。
如果把原本靠近平衡位置的分子稍微拉开，吸引就占优势，合力会促使它们靠近。

在小而可恢复的弹性形变范围内，外界作用停止后，这种恢复作用使分子趋向初始位置。
这不表示任意远离的分子都会自行返回，物体若已断裂也不适用这个结论。

当分子间的距离超过分子本身大小的几倍时，在这里讨论的中性分子模型中，相互作用通常已很弱，实际上可以忽略。
这种力因此称为短程作用力，并不是说它在某个距离处突然变成零。

分子只偏离平衡位置很小时，无论吸引还是排斥占优势，合力都指向平衡位置，其大小近似随偏离距离线性增大。
图 $5$ 中合力曲线的粗线段很短，可以近似看作直线段。

因此，在小形变的弹性范围内，胡克定律近似成立，即弹性力的大小与形变成正比。
分子偏离平衡位置较大时，曲线的弯曲不能忽略，胡克定律的线性近似就不再适用。

物体发生形变时，许多相邻分子层之间的距离都会改变，总形变分散在这些分子层之间。
只要分到每一层的距离变化仍很小，局部的线性近似就仍然适用。

因此，即使物体的总形变超过分子大小的百万倍，胡克定律仍可能成立，条件是形变仍在弹性范围内。
总形变的长度很大，不代表每一层的距离变化也很大。
fullText.en:
A thick wooden stick is hard to break, showing that the forces between its atoms or molecules can be strong.
The stick, too, is made of molecules.
Any attempt to break it should be handled safely by an adult, with care to avoid splinters and flying fragments.

In the simplified molecular model discussed here, molecules without mutual attraction could not gather into liquids or solids and would remain dispersed like a gas.
Attraction keeps molecules close together and is an important condition for forming liquids and solids.

Attraction alone, however, cannot keep the arrangement of atoms and molecules stable.
Repulsion becomes strong when molecules are very close.
It resists further compression and prevents them from being pushed indefinitely into one another.

Atoms contain electrons and nuclei, while molecules have still more complex structures built from atoms.
Electrons and nuclei carry electric charge, so those in neighboring molecules interact.

Even a molecule with no overall charge can have strong electrical interactions at short distances.
Describing the motion of these particles and the forces between molecules is a complex problem studied in atomic physics.

A full account requires quantum theory, not just a picture of fixed electric charges.
Here we use the results of that theory only to outline how the force between two molecules depends on their center-to-center distance.

Atoms and molecules contain particles with opposite electric charges.
In this simplified model, their interactions are represented by an attractive part and a repulsive part.

These parts act in opposite directions.
With the direction of repulsion taken as positive, the net force component is the repulsive magnitude minus the attractive magnitude, and its sign gives the direction.

Within the short-distance range described by this model, repulsion increases faster than attraction as atoms move closer together①.
Repulsion rises especially steeply when the electron shells of atoms or molecules begin to overlap.

① More precisely, we are comparing the components of the forces along the line joining the centers of the two atoms.
These signed components indicate direction along that line.

Figure $5$ sketches the approximate dependence of repulsion (upper curve), attraction (lower curve), and the net force (middle curve) on the distance between molecular centers.
Taking repulsion as the positive direction along the line of centers makes the repulsive component positive and the attractive component negative.

In this model, the equilibrium distance is approximately the sum of the two molecular radii, $r_0$, where the two force magnitudes are equal and the net force is $F=0$.
When $r>r_0$, attraction is stronger, so $F<0$ and the net force pulls the molecules closer together.

If $r\to\infty$, then $F\to0$: the interaction tends to zero as the separation tends to infinity.
When $r<r_0$, repulsion is stronger, so $F>0$ and the net force pushes the molecules apart.

Figure 5

The way the net intermolecular force varies with distance helps explain elastic forces in a compressed or stretched body.
If compression reduces the molecular separation below $r_0$, repulsion is stronger and the net force resists further approach.

If molecules initially near equilibrium are pulled slightly apart, attraction is stronger and the net force draws them closer.
For a small, recoverable elastic deformation, this restoring action tends to bring the molecules back toward their initial positions after the external action stops.
This does not mean that arbitrarily distant molecules will return on their own, or that the same conclusion applies to a broken body.

In this model of neutral molecules, the interaction usually becomes negligible when their separation is more than several times their size.
Intermolecular forces of this kind are short-range forces, meaning that they rapidly become weak rather than stopping abruptly at a fixed distance.

When molecules move only a little from equilibrium, the net force points back toward equilibrium.
Its magnitude grows approximately in proportion to the displacement, whether attraction or repulsion is stronger.

The short, thick segment of the net-force curve in Figure $5$ can therefore be treated as approximately straight.
Thus Hooke's law is a useful approximation for small elastic deformations: the magnitude of the elastic force is proportional to the deformation.
For larger molecular displacements, the curve's bending matters and this linear approximation no longer applies.

When a body deforms, the separations of many neighboring molecular layers change, distributing the total deformation across those layers.
The change between any pair of neighboring layers can therefore remain very small.

This is why Hooke's law can still apply even when the total deformation exceeds a million times the size of a molecule, provided each layer's change stays small and the deformation remains elastic.
A large total change in length does not mean a large change in each intermolecular separation.
fullText.originalZh:
证明原子或分子间存在有很大的相互作用力，是不复杂的。请试一试把粗棍子折断！要知道，它是由分子组成的。

假如分子间没有吸引力，那么所有物质在任何条件下都只能处于气态。只是由于分子间的吸引力，才能保持它们彼此靠近，从而形成液体和固体。只有吸引力还不能保证原子和分子处于稳定形态。分子间距离很小时，它们之间还有排斥力。由于排斥力的存在，分子间才不能彼此侵透。

原子，尤其分子，也是一个复杂的系统，它是由单个的带电粒子：电子和原子核组成的。虽然分子的整体是中性的，但在距离很小时它们之间有很大的电力。相邻分子的电子和原子核之间有相互作用。描写原子和分子内部粒子的运动和分子间的作用力，是一个很复杂的问题；在原子物理学中研究这个问题。这里只是根据原子物理学的研究结果，说明一下两个分子相互作用力与它们之间距离的大致关系。

因为原子和分子是由带相反符号电荷的粒子组成的，所以，原子之间和分子之间同时存在有吸引力和排斥力。分子间作用的合力等于这两个力大小的差。

当原子间的距离减小时，吸引力比排斥力增大得慢①，当原子（或分子）的电子层开始重合时，排斥力增长得特别快。

①　准确地说，这里不应当说力，而应说力在两个原子中心联线上的投影。

图 $5$ 描绘了排斥力（上面的曲线）、吸引力（下面的曲线）和合力（中间的曲线）与分子中心之间的距离的大致关系。排斥力为正的，而吸引力是负的。当分子间的距离大约等于两个分子半径之和 $r_0$ 时，合力 $F=0$，因为吸引力等于排斥力。当$r>r_0$ 时，吸引力大于排斥力，从而 $F<0$。如果 $r\to\infty$，那么$F\to0$。当距离 $r<r_0$ 时，排斥力大于吸引力，从而 $F>0$。

图 5

分子相互作用力与它们之间的距离的关系，可以解释当物体压缩和拉伸时出现的弹性力。如果迫使分子间的距离小于 $r_0$，就产生阻碍接近的力。相反，当分子被扯远离时，就产生了吸引力，当外界作用停止之后，这个吸引力使分子回到初始位置。

如果分子间的距离超过它们的大小几倍，那么分子间的相互作用实际上就不明显了。分子力是短程作用力。

当分子移开平衡位置很小时，吸引力或排斥力随着位移的增大而线性地增大。曲线上很小的一段可以认为是直线段（图 $5$ 上曲线的粗线段）。因此，当形变小的时候，胡克定律是正确的，即弹性力与形变成正比。当分子移动大时，胡克定律就不正确了。

因为当物体形变时，所有分子之间的距离都改变，所以，总的形变分到相邻分子层上的是很小的。因此，当形变超过分子大小的百万倍时，胡克定律仍然成立。
